Introduction and Learning Objectives¶

Translate logical statements into binary constraints, model continuous alternatives with Pyomo.GDP, and compare Big-M and hull reformulations. The separator and parts examples develop the logic; the reactor example shows how bounds affect the reformulation. Full derivations and reproducible diagnostics supplement the lecture activities.

Motivating Example: Separation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.7 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

Black circles mark the common binary vertices; squares mark the two extra aggregate vertices. The slice exposes the printed fractional witness.

If the absorber is selected or the membrane is selected, do not use cryogenic separation. Let yA,yM,yCS∈{0,1}y_A,y_M,y_{CS}\in\{0,1\}yA​,yM​,yCS​∈{0,1} indicate these selections. The OR is inclusive: selecting both absorber and membrane is permitted.

Translate each way the antecedent can be true first:

yA+yCS≤1,yM+yCS≤1.y_A+y_{CS}\le1,\qquad y_M+y_{CS}\le1.yA​+yCS​≤1,yM​+yCS​≤1.
(1)

Adding the two rows gives the aggregate:

yA+yM+2yCS≤2.y_A+y_M+2y_{CS}\le2.yA​+yM​+2yCS​≤2.
(2)

The pair implies the aggregate even for fractional variables. Conversely, for binary variables the aggregate enforces both rows: if yCS=1y_{CS}=1yCS​=1, it forces yA=yM=0y_A=y_M=0yA​=yM​=0; if yCS=0y_{CS}=0yCS​=0, it imposes no further restriction. Thus both formulations describe the same binary choices.

They differ on the unit cube [0,1]3[0,1]^3[0,1]3. At (yA,yM,yCS)=(1,0,1/2)(y_A,y_M,y_{CS})=(1,0,1/2)(yA​,yM​,yCS​)=(1,0,1/2), the aggregate holds with equality, but the first pairwise row reads 3/2≤13/2\le13/2≤1 and fails. The pair therefore has a strictly tighter LP relaxation. The all-zero choice remains feasible: the implication does not require installing a separator.

Source: Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997), §15.7, pp. 514–517, Example 15.4.

Logical Modeling¶

An atomic statement can represent a selection, such as “use the absorber.” Logical connectives combine these statements. Conjunctive normal form separates the resulting formula into disjunctive clauses, each of which becomes one linear inequality.

Symbolic Logic Notation¶

Logical OperationLogical Symbol
OR\text{OR}OR∨\lor∨
AND\text{AND}AND∧\land∧
IMPLICATION\text{IMPLICATION}IMPLICATION⇒\Rightarrow⇒
NEGATION\text{NEGATION}NEGATION¬\neg¬
EQUIVALENCE\text{EQUIVALENCE}EQUIVALENCE⇔\Leftrightarrow⇔
EXCLUSIVE OR\text{EXCLUSIVE OR}EXCLUSIVE OR⊻\veebar⊻

Vocabulary¶

An atom PiP_iPi​ has no logical connective inside it. Associate the binary variable yi=1y_i=1yi​=1 with a true atom and yi=0y_i=0yi​=0 with a false atom. A literal is an atom PiP_iPi​ or its negation ¬Pi\neg P_i¬Pi​; their numerical truth values are yiy_iyi​ and 1−yi1-y_i1−yi​.

A disjunctive clause is an OR of finitely many literals. It is true when at least one literal is true. A conjunctive clause is an AND of literals; all must be true. Conjunctive normal form (CNF) is an AND of disjunctive clauses, not an arbitrary sequence of clauses.

For example,

Q=(P1∨¬P2∨P3)∧(¬P1∨P4)Q=(P_1\lor\neg P_2\lor P_3)\land(\neg P_1\lor P_4)Q=(P1​∨¬P2​∨P3​)∧(¬P1​∨P4​)
(3)

is CNF and translates to

y1+(1−y2)+y3≥1,(1−y1)+y4≥1.y_1+(1-y_2)+y_3\ge1,\qquad(1-y_1)+y_4\ge1.y1​+(1−y2​)+y3​≥1,(1−y1​)+y4​≥1.
(4)

More generally, if a clause has positive-literal indices J+J^+J+ and negative-literal indices J−J^-J−, its row is

∑j∈J+yj+∑j∈J−(1−yj)≥1.\sum_{j\in J^+}y_j+\sum_{j\in J^-}(1-y_j)\ge1.j∈J+∑​yj​+j∈J−∑​(1−yj​)≥1.
(5)

Each literal is 0 or 1, so this sum is at least one exactly when the clause is true. Retain binary domains: this equivalence concerns truth assignments, not fractional truth values.

Example: Assembling Components¶

If (parts 1 and 2) or part 3 is used, then parts 4 or 5 must also be used. Here PiP_iPi​ means “use part iii,” and both ORs are inclusive.

((P1∧P2)∨P3)⇒(P4∨P5).((P_1\land P_2)\lor P_3)\Rightarrow(P_4\lor P_5).((P1​∧P2​)∨P3​)⇒(P4​∨P5​).
(14)

Step 1: replace the implication. Apply A⇒B⇔¬A∨BA\Rightarrow B\Leftrightarrow\neg A\lor BA⇒B⇔¬A∨B with the whole antecedent A=((P1∧P2)∨P3)A=((P_1\land P_2)\lor P_3)A=((P1​∧P2​)∨P3​) and B=(P4∨P5)B=(P_4\lor P_5)B=(P4​∨P5​):

¬((P1∧P2)∨P3)∨(P4∨P5).\neg((P_1\land P_2)\lor P_3)\lor(P_4\lor P_5).¬((P1​∧P2​)∨P3​)∨(P4​∨P5​).
(15)

Step 2: move the negations inward. De Morgan’s laws first negate the outer OR and then the inner AND:

[¬(P1∧P2)∧¬P3]∨(P4∨P5)[\neg(P_1\land P_2)\land\neg P_3]\lor(P_4\lor P_5)[¬(P1​∧P2​)∧¬P3​]∨(P4​∨P5​)
(16)
[(¬P1∨¬P2)∧¬P3]∨(P4∨P5).[(\neg P_1\lor\neg P_2)\land\neg P_3]\lor(P_4\lor P_5).[(¬P1​∨¬P2​)∧¬P3​]∨(P4​∨P5​).
(17)

Step 3: distribute OR over AND. With C=(P4∨P5)C=(P_4\lor P_5)C=(P4​∨P5​), distribute (A∧B)∨C(A\land B)\lor C(A∧B)∨C into (A∨C)∧(B∨C)(A\lor C)\land(B\lor C)(A∨C)∧(B∨C):

(¬P1∨¬P2∨P4∨P5)∧(¬P3∨P4∨P5).(\neg P_1\lor\neg P_2\lor P_4\lor P_5)\land(\neg P_3\lor P_4\lor P_5).(¬P1​∨¬P2​∨P4​∨P5​)∧(¬P3​∨P4​∨P5​).
(18)

Translate the two clauses separately:

(1−y1)+(1−y2)+y4+y5≥1,(1-y_1)+(1-y_2)+y_4+y_5\ge1,(1−y1​)+(1−y2​)+y4​+y5​≥1,
(19)
(1−y3)+y4+y5≥1.(1-y_3)+y_4+y_5\ge1.(1−y3​)+y4​+y5​≥1.
(20)

Equivalently,

y1+y2−y4−y5≤1,y3−y4−y5≤0.y_1+y_2-y_4-y_5\le1,\qquad y_3-y_4-y_5\le0.y1​+y2​−y4​−y5​≤1,y3​−y4​−y5​≤0.
(21)

The first row has y4y_4y4​, not y3y_3y3​, in its negative terms. For example, parts 1 and 2 without 4 or 5 must be rejected even when part 3 is absent. Source: BGW, Example 15.5, Eqs. (15.28)–(15.33), pp. 516–517.

Modeling Disjunctions¶

When modeling disjunctions, we will have to represent logical constraints that involve continuous variables.

General Notation¶

A generalized disjunctive program combines an objective, global algebraic constraints, disjunctions, and logical constraints. One common form is

min⁡x,c,Yf(x)+∑k∈Kcksubject tog(x)≤0,L≤x≤U,⋁i∈Dk[Yikgik(x)≤0ck=γik],k∈K,Ω(Y)=True,Yik∈{False,True}.\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c},Y}\quad & f(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{k\in K}c_k\\ \text{subject to}\quad &\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})\le\mathbf{0},\qquad \mathbf{L}\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{U},\\ &\bigvee_{i\in D_k}\begin{bmatrix}Y_{ik}\\\mathbf{g}_{ik}(\mathbf{x})\le\mathbf{0}\\c_k=\gamma_{ik}\end{bmatrix},\quad k\in K,\\ &\Omega(Y)=\mathrm{True},\qquad Y_{ik}\in\{\mathrm{False},\mathrm{True}\}. \end{aligned}x,c,Ymin​subject to​f(x)+k∈K∑​ck​g(x)≤0,L≤x≤U,i∈Dk​⋁​⎣⎡​Yik​gik​(x)≤0ck​=γik​​⎦⎤​,k∈K,Ω(Y)=True,Yik​∈{False,True}.​
(22)

Here KKK indexes disjunctions and DkD_kDk​ indexes the alternatives in disjunction kkk. The cost variable ckc_kck​ is assigned the given cost γik\gamma_{ik}γik​ when term iii is selected. Each selected term enforces all its constraints together. Global rows hold regardless of the choice. The Boolean indicators YikY_{ik}Yik​ are distinct from their algebraic binary representatives yiky_{ik}yik​.

The displayed ⋁\bigvee⋁ denotes inclusive OR. Our reactor and packing models additionally impose exactly one selected indicator per disjunction, which is Pyomo’s default. A false indicator removes that term’s requirements; it does not assert the negation of every inequality in the term. Thus more than one alternative’s algebraic inequalities can happen to hold even though only one indicator is selected.

Sources: Bynum et al. (2021), §11.1, Eqs. (11.13)–(11.17), p. 173; Pyomo’s modeling documentation. Pyomo exposes indicator_var as Boolean and binary_indicator_var as its associated binary. Use BooleanVar for logic and a Var(domain=Binary) for numeric binary algebra.

Example: The Reactor Problem¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

This modeling disjunctions example involves selecting between two reactors:

  • If reactor 1 is selected, then pressure PPP must be between 5 and 10 atmospheres.

  • If reactor 2 is selected, then pressure PPP must be between 20 and 30 atmospheres.

A bounded linear disjunction has term sets

Si={x:Aix≤bi, L≤x≤U},i∈D.S_i=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}_i,\ \mathbf{L}\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{U}\},\qquad i\in D.Si​={x:Ai​x≤bi​, L≤x≤U},i∈D.
(23)

Selecting a term enforces all of its rows. With exactly-one selection, eliminating the indicators leaves the union ⋃i∈DSi\bigcup_{i\in D}S_i⋃i∈D​Si​. The same continuous union can also be represented by inclusive selection; overlapping terms can then have several true indicators.

Applied to the reactor problem:

[Y15≤P≤10]∨[Y220≤P≤30],y1+y2=1.\begin{bmatrix}Y_1\\5\le P\le10\end{bmatrix}\lor\begin{bmatrix}Y_2\\20\le P\le30\end{bmatrix},\qquad y_1+y_2=1.[Y1​5≤P≤10​]∨[Y2​20≤P≤30​],y1​+y2​=1.
(24)

The continuous feasible set is [5,10]∪[20,30][5,10]\cup[20,30][5,10]∪[20,30] atm. We minimize PPP to obtain a simple test objective. The analytic Big-M illustration below uses the declared common box 0≤P≤300\le P\le300≤P≤30. The canonical Pyomo builder uses the stronger valid bound 5≤P≤305\le P\le305≤P≤30. This difference affects automatic Big-M values and LP bounds; it does not change the original disjunctive feasible set.

Define Model in Pyomo with GDP¶

First we will define the model (including disjunctions) for the Reactor Problem in Pyomo.

"""
Instead of using
# import pyomo.environ as pyo
We can import specific functions/objects
"""

from pyomo.environ import (
    check_optimal_termination,
    ConcreteModel,
    Param,
    Set,
    SolverFactory,
    TransformationFactory,
    Var,
)
def add_pressure_windows(model):
    # One exactly-one disjunction, with both pressure rows in each term.
    # GDP creates the indicators; reformulation supplies the algebraic rows.
    @model.Disjunction(
        doc="Select exactly one reactor; each brings its own pressure window"
    )
    def pressure_bounds(b):
        # Two inner lists: one simultaneous pressure window per reactor.
        return [
            [b.P <= b.max_pressure[r], b.P >= b.min_pressure[r]] for r in b.reactors
        ]


def create_model():
    """
    Build the reactor problem model.

    Return:
    model: Pyomo model

    """
    ## Model
    model = ConcreteModel(name="Selecting a reactor")

    ## Sets
    # Initialized for reactor 1 (1) and reactor 2 (2)
    model.reactors = Set(initialize=[1, 2])

    ## Parameters
    # Initialized with a dictionary where the keys are 1 and 2 (the reactors)
    # for the minimum and maximum pressure values (atm)
    model.min_pressure = Param(model.reactors, initialize={1: 5, 2: 20})
    model.max_pressure = Param(model.reactors, initialize={1: 10, 2: 30})

    ## Variables
    # Reactor pressure bounded between the lower bound (5 atm) and upper bound (30 atm).
    # These bounds are what gdp.bigm reads to compute M per row -- here 20, 0, 0, 15.
    # Automatic M estimation needs finite expression bounds; valid supplied M values
    # are an alternative. Hull requires finite bounds on variables in its disjuncts.
    model.P = Var(bounds=(5, 30), doc="Reactor pressure (atm)")

    ## Adding an objective for the example
    @model.Objective()
    def objective(b):
        return b.P

    add_pressure_windows(model)

    return model
Warning

The nesting matters. @model.Disjunction returns a list of disjuncts, and each disjunct is itself a list of constraints that hold together. Here that is a list of two lists: one per reactor, each carrying both of that reactor’s pressure bounds.

Flatten it, or index the decorator over model.reactors, and Pyomo builds a different model. Indexing over the reactors gives two disjunctions --- “for reactor 1, either P≤10P \leq 10P≤10 or P≥5P \geq 5P≥5” and “for reactor 2, either P≤30P \leq 30P≤30 or P≥20P \geq 20P≥20” --- neither of which restricts PPP at all, since P∈[5,30]P \in [5, 30]P∈[5,30] already satisfies one branch of each. That model admits P=15P = 15P=15, which the disjunction forbids.

This error is invisible in the minimum below: the objective is min⁡P\min PminP, and both the right model and the wrong one return P=5P = 5P=5. Check a model by asking what it excludes, not only what it returns.

Pyomo creates the Boolean and associated binary indicators when the disjuncts are declared, as the pre-transformation model printout shows. Reformulation then supplies the algebraic selection and constraint rows.

Transform and Solve with Big-M Relaxation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

Use “Big-M” constraints to convert linear disjunctions into mixed-integer constraints to represent logic with continuous variables.

Big-M Relaxation Approach¶

For each row aijTx≤bija_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}\le b_{ij}aijT​x≤bij​ in term iii, choose a nonnegative constant MijM_{ij}Mij​ large enough that the row imposes no restriction on the relevant off-state domain:

aijTx≤bij+Mij(1−yi),∑i∈Dyi=1,yi∈{0,1}.a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}\le b_{ij}+M_{ij}(1-y_i),\qquad\sum_{i\in D}y_i=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}.aijT​x≤bij​+Mij​(1−yi​),i∈D∑​yi​=1,yi​∈{0,1}.
(25)

When yi=1y_i=1yi​=1, the original row is enforced. When yi=0y_i=0yi​=0, a valid MijM_{ij}Mij​ deactivates it. A conservative choice is

Mij≥max⁡{0, max⁡L≤x≤U(aijTx−bij)}.M_{ij}\ge\max\left\{0,\ \max_{\mathbf{L}\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{U}}(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}-b_{ij})\right\}.Mij​≥max{0, L≤x≤Umax​(aijT​x−bij​)}.
(26)

A common constant for all rows of a term can be the maximum of their row constants. Bounds or constraints known to hold in the other selected terms may yield smaller valid constants. State which off-state domain was used.

For the reactor, common constants give

P≤10+M1(1−y1),−P≤−5+M1(1−y1),P≤30+M2(1−y2),−P≤−20+M2(1−y2),y1+y2=1,y1,y2∈{0,1}.\begin{aligned} P&\le10+M_1(1-y_1),& -P&\le-5+M_1(1-y_1),\\ P&\le30+M_2(1-y_2),& -P&\le-20+M_2(1-y_2),\\ y_1+y_2&=1,& y_1,y_2&\in\{0,1\}. \end{aligned}PPy1​+y2​​≤10+M1​(1−y1​),≤30+M2​(1−y2​),=1,​−P−Py1​,y2​​≤−5+M1​(1−y1​),≤−20+M2​(1−y2​),∈{0,1}.​
(27)

Over the entire box [0,30][0,30][0,30], maximum row violations are 20,5,0,2020,5,0,2020,5,0,20, so M1=M2=20M_1=M_2=20M1​=M2​=20 deactivates every row over that box. These are the smallest common per-term constants for that deactivation policy. They are not the smallest constants that can preserve this particular union: when term 2 is off, term 1 supplies P≥5P\ge5P≥5, so M2=15M_2=15M2​=15 already suffices.

A too-small constant may remove feasible points. For example, M1=10M_1=10M1​=10 wrongly caps P≤20P\le20P≤20 when reactor 2 is selected, cutting out its valid pressures above 20. An unnecessarily large constant can weaken the LP relaxation and worsen scaling; it does not guarantee a particular iteration count. Neither problem size alone nor a blanket preference selects the better reformulation.

Source: BGW, §15.8, Eqs. (15.43)–(15.44), pp. 519–520. The two printing errors in (15.44) are corrected above: the fourth row starts with -20, and the selection row is y1+y2=1y_1+y_2=1y1​+y2​=1.

Transform and Solve with Convex Hull Relaxation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

The linear hull construction disaggregates each continuous variable into one scaled copy per term. The copies express a convex combination of feasible points, giving the convex hull of one bounded linear disjunction when the indicators are relaxed. This avoids choosing Big-M constants, at the cost of additional variables and rows.

Convex Hull Relaxation Approach¶

This analytic illustration uses the manual box-wide constants, not the automatic transformation of the builder with P bounded below by 5. The hatched difference is entirely at the lower boundary.

For the nonempty bounded linear term sets SiS_iSi​ defined above, introduce zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ and impose

x=∑i∈Dzi,Aizi≤biyi,i∈D,Lyi≤zi≤Uyi,i∈D,∑i∈Dyi=1,yi∈{0,1}.\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}&=\sum_{i\in D}\mathbf{z}_i,\\ \mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{z}_i&\le\mathbf{b}_i y_i,\qquad i\in D,\\ \mathbf{L}y_i&\le\mathbf{z}_i\le\mathbf{U}y_i,\qquad i\in D,\\ \sum_{i\in D}y_i&=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \end{aligned}xAi​zi​Lyi​i∈D∑​yi​​=i∈D∑​zi​,≤bi​yi​,i∈D,≤zi​≤Uyi​,i∈D,=1,yi​∈{0,1}.​
(28)

The bounds are signed: L\mathbf{L}L need not be zero. For example, a valid selected value x=−1x=-1x=−1 would be lost if 0≤zi0\le z_i0≤zi​ were incorrectly imposed. At yi=0y_i=0yi​=0, the scaled bounds force zi=0\mathbf{z}_i=\mathbf{0}zi​=0. The row Aizi≤0\mathbf{A}_i\mathbf{z}_i\le\mathbf{0}Ai​zi​≤0 alone need not do so; −zi≤0-z_i\le0−zi​≤0 allows any nonnegative ziz_izi​.

Why the relaxed formulation gives the hull. Replace binary domains by yi≥0y_i\ge0yi​≥0. For any positive weight yiy_iyi​, divide by that weight to obtain zi/yi∈Si\mathbf{z}_i/y_i\in S_izi​/yi​∈Si​. The zero-weight copies vanish by the scaled bounds. Hence x=∑i:yi>0yi(zi/yi)\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i:y_i>0}y_i(\mathbf{z}_i/y_i)x=∑i:yi​>0​yi​(zi​/yi​) is a convex combination of points in the union. Conversely, combine any convex combination’s contributions from the same term, which is convex; assigning its total weight to yiy_iyi​ and its weighted point to zi\mathbf{z}_izi​ satisfies every row. This proves both inclusions.

With binary weights, exactly one copy remains and equals x\mathbf{x}x, proving exactness for the original union. The bounded linear assumptions matter: nonlinear hull reformulation needs additional theory. Also, intersecting separately convexified disjunctions with global constraints need not give the convex hull of the entire GDP feasible set.

Reactor hull:

P=P1+P2,5y1≤P1≤10y1,20y2≤P2≤30y2,y1+y2=1,y1,y2∈{0,1}.\begin{aligned} P&=P_1+P_2,\\ 5y_1\le P_1&\le10y_1,\qquad20y_2\le P_2\le30y_2,\\ y_1+y_2&=1,\qquad y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}. \end{aligned}P5y1​≤P1​y1​+y2​​=P1​+P2​,≤10y1​,20y2​≤P2​≤30y2​,=1,y1​,y2​∈{0,1}.​
(29)

Here each term already bounds its copy on both sides, forcing an off-copy to zero. With t=y1t=y_1t=y1​, y2=1−ty_2=1-ty2​=1−t, the relaxed pressure interval is

20−15t≤P≤30−20t,0≤t≤1.20-15t\le P\le30-20t,\qquad0\le t\le1.20−15t≤P≤30−20t,0≤t≤1.
(30)

Every value in this interval is a sum of points in [5t,10t][5t,10t][5t,10t] and [20(1−t),30(1−t)][20(1-t),30(1-t)][20(1−t),30(1−t)]. Thus these projected bounds are necessary and sufficient. Minimizing PPP gives 5.

For the manual [0,30][0,30][0,30], M1=M2=20M_1=M_2=20M1​=M2​=20 model, the corresponding lower bound is max⁡{20t−15,20−20t}\max\{20t-15,20-20t\}max{20t−15,20−20t} and the upper bound is 30−20t30-20t30−20t. The lower lines meet at t=7/8t=7/8t=7/8, P=5/2P=5/2P=5/2, whereas the hull’s lower bound there is 55/855/855/8. At t=1/2t=1/2t=1/2, the respective intervals are [10,20][10,20][10,20] and [12.5,20][12.5,20][12.5,20]. The upper boundaries agree; the lower boundaries explain the gap.

Sources: BGW, Eqs. (15.45)–(15.46), pp. 520–521; Balas (1985). Pyomo’s hull transformation requires finite lower and upper bounds on the variables appearing in disjuncts, including when automatic Big-M estimation could instead be replaced by supplied valid constants.

Discussion Questions¶

  1. Why does CNF allow one linear row per clause?

  2. Does the separator implication require selecting any separator?

  3. What changes when an indicator is zero in Big-M? Does it assert the opposite inequality?

  4. Is hull always strictly stronger than a valid Big-M formulation?

  5. Under what conditions can the zero-term hull be simplified?

Answers

  1. Each clause is an OR of literals. Its sum of binary truth values must be at least one; an AND of clauses requires every such row.

  2. No. The all-zero selection makes the antecedent false and satisfies the implication. Add a separate selection requirement if the process needs one.

  3. A valid constant makes the term’s row nonrestrictive on the relevant off-state domain. The false indicator does not enforce the negation of that row.

  4. No. It can be stronger, or the LP relaxations can agree. The following diagnostics show equality for this notebook’s automatically bounded reactor model.

  5. The particular two-term on/off construction below eliminates the off-copy. This is not a theorem that every two-term GDP simplifies in the same way.

Check the model and its relaxations¶

The following calculation constructs fresh copies of the same builder used above, inspects Pyomo’s signed lower/upper M values, and solves their MIP and LP versions. It also checks a pressure cap of 19: the correct model must return 10, not 19. Fixing P=15P=15P=15 must be infeasible. Both checks detect an error that the minimum P=5P=5P=5 would miss.

For this builder’s box [5,30][5,30][5,30], automatic row magnitudes are 20,0,0,1520,0,0,1520,0,0,15. Substitution yields 20−15t≤P≤30−20t20-15t\le P\le30-20t20−15t≤P≤30−20t, the same projection as the hull. A zero M means the bound is already globally implied. This example therefore illustrates equality, rather than a strict automatic-Big-M/hull gap. The manual M=20M=20M=20 illustration deliberately uses a different deactivation policy.

import json
import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.gdp import Disjunction
import pyomo

def model_size(m):
    variables = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Var, active=True))
    rows = list(m.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True))
    return {"continuous_variables": sum(not v.is_binary() for v in variables),
            "binary_variables": sum(v.is_binary() for v in variables),
            "equalities": sum(c.equality for c in rows),
            "inequalities": sum(not c.equality for c in rows)}

def reactor_check(transform, relax=False, cap=None, fixed_pressure=None):
    m = create_model()
    if cap is not None:
        m.cap = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.P <= cap)
        m.objective.sense = pyo.maximize
    if fixed_pressure is not None:
        m.P.fix(fixed_pressure)
    reformulation = pyo.TransformationFactory(transform)
    reformulation.apply_to(m)
    size = model_size(m)
    M_values = None
    if transform == "gdp.bigm":
        M_values = {c.name: list(pair) for c, pair in
                    reformulation.get_all_M_values_by_constraint(m).items()}
    if relax:
        pyo.TransformationFactory("core.relax_integer_vars").apply_to(m)
    solver = pyo.SolverFactory(milp_solver)
    solved = solver.solve(m, load_solutions=False)
    termination = str(solved.solver.termination_condition)
    pressure = None
    if pyo.check_optimal_termination(solved):
        m.solutions.load_from(solved)
        pressure = pyo.value(m.P)
    return {"transformation": transform, "LP": relax, "cap": cap,
            "fixed_pressure": fixed_pressure, "termination": termination,
            "pressure": pressure, "size_before_relaxing": size, "signed_M": M_values}

reactor_diagnostics = [reactor_check(t, relax=r)
                       for t in ("gdp.bigm", "gdp.hull") for r in (False, True)]
reactor_diagnostics += [reactor_check("gdp.bigm", cap=19),
                        reactor_check("gdp.bigm", fixed_pressure=15)]
assert all(abs(row["pressure"] - 5) < 1e-8 for row in reactor_diagnostics[:4])
assert abs(reactor_diagnostics[4]["pressure"] - 10) < 1e-8
assert reactor_diagnostics[5]["termination"] == "infeasible"
print("Pyomo", pyomo.__version__)
print(json.dumps(reactor_diagnostics, indent=2))

A test that rejects the toothless indexed model¶

The incorrect formulation below creates two independent exactly-one choices between overlapping half-lines. At P=15P=15P=15, each pair has a satisfied alternative. Even exclusive indicator selection cannot repair a wrongly grouped model: the unselected half-line is deactivated, rather than negated.

wrong = pyo.ConcreteModel()
wrong.P = pyo.Var(bounds=(5, 30))
@wrong.Disjunction([1, 2])
def pressure_bounds(b, r):
    lo, hi = {1: (5, 10), 2: (20, 30)}[r]
    return [b.P <= hi, b.P >= lo]
wrong.cap = pyo.Constraint(expr=wrong.P <= 19)
wrong.objective = pyo.Objective(expr=wrong.P, sense=pyo.maximize)
pyo.TransformationFactory("gdp.bigm").apply_to(wrong)
wrong_result = pyo.SolverFactory(milp_solver).solve(wrong)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(wrong_result)
assert abs(pyo.value(wrong.P) - 19) < 1e-8
wrong.P.fix(15)
wrong_result = pyo.SolverFactory(milp_solver).solve(wrong)
assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(wrong_result)
print("Incorrect indexed model: max P with P <= 19 is 19; P = 15 is feasible.")
Incorrect indexed model: max P with P <= 19 is 19; P = 15 is feasible.

Reproduce the manual LP bounds¶

The following LPs use the same four reactor rows with explicit nonnegative row constants. Their continuous variables are (P,t)(P,t)(P,t), with y1=ty_1=ty1​=t and y2=1−ty_2=1-ty2​=1−t. Keeping the box and constant policy in the output makes the comparison reproducible.

For [0,30][0,30][0,30], row-specific box maxima (20,5,0,20)(20,5,0,20)(20,5,0,20) improve the LP bound from 2.5 to 4. Using the other branch to justify common constants (M1,M2)=(20,15)(M_1,M_2)=(20,15)(M1​,M2​)=(20,15) gives the hull projection and bound 5. The canonical [5,30][5,30][5,30] automatic constants (20,0,0,15)(20,0,0,15)(20,0,0,15) also give 5. These choices are all valid for integer selections; their fractional behavior differs.

from scipy.optimize import linprog

manual_lp_bounds = []
for label, lower, M in (
    ("box [0,30], common M=20", 0, (20,20,20,20)),
    ("box [0,30], row-specific box maxima", 0, (20,5,0,20)),
    ("box [0,30], other-branch common M", 0, (20,20,15,15)),
    ("box [5,30], automatic row magnitudes", 5, (20,0,0,15)),
):
    u1,l1,u2,l2 = M
    # Columns are (P,t): upper/lower reactor-1 rows, then reactor-2 rows.
    A = [[1,u1],[-1,l1],[1,-u2],[-1,-l2]]
    b = [10+u1,-5+l1,30,-20]
    lp = linprog([1,0], A_ub=A, b_ub=b, bounds=[(lower,30),(0,1)], method="highs")
    assert lp.success
    manual_lp_bounds.append({"case": label, "row_M": list(M),
                             "minimum_P": float(lp.fun), "t": float(lp.x[1])})
assert all(abs(row["minimum_P"]-expected)<1e-8
           for row,expected in zip(manual_lp_bounds,(2.5,4,5,5)))
print(json.dumps(manual_lp_bounds, indent=2))

Formulation size and choice¶

For one disjunction with ddd terms, nnn continuous components, and rir_iri​ inequalities in term iii, count the algebraic core as follows. These are numbers of declared components, not a Jacobian rank or degrees-of-freedom calculation.

ComponentCommon-per-term Big-MLinear hull
Continuous variablesnnnn+ndn+ndn+nd
Binary indicatorsdddddd
Equalities1 selection row1 selection row and nnn linking rows
Term inequalities∑iri\sum_i r_i∑i​ri​∑iri\sum_i r_i∑i​ri​

This table excludes domain bounds and scaled-copy bound rows. The explicit general hull also has 2nd2nd2nd scaled bound inequalities, although some can be redundant or subsumed by term rows. Global constraints add to both formulations. Pyomo can eliminate or reuse components, so compare the actual counts printed above under a stated convention rather than asserting they must equal the simplified table.

Tighter relaxations can improve lower bounds for minimization, while larger models cost more per node. Bounds, formulation structure, presolve, objective, and solver all matter. Compare actual relaxations and solve evidence; “Big-M for small problems, hull for large problems” is not a valid selection rule. This notebook reports optimality and mathematical bounds rather than treating an iteration count as a universal performance result.

Source: BGW, §15.8, p. 521. Nonlinear convex hull theory is treated by Grossmann & Lee (2003); it does not follow from the bounded linear proof above.

A two-term on/off simplification¶

Consider [Y; Ax≤b, L≤x≤U][Y;\ \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{L}\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{U}][Y; Ax≤b, L≤x≤U] or [¬Y; x=0][\neg Y;\ \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}][¬Y; x=0]. The hull copies satisfy x=zon+zoff\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}_{on}+\mathbf{z}_{off}x=zon​+zoff​ and zoff=0\mathbf{z}_{off}=\mathbf{0}zoff​=0, so eliminate both copies to obtain

Ax≤by,Ly≤x≤Uy,y∈{0,1}.\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}y,\qquad\mathbf{L}y\le\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{U}y,\qquad y\in\{0,1\}.Ax≤by,Ly≤x≤Uy,y∈{0,1}.
(31)

At y=1y=1y=1 these are the original on-term rows; at y=0y=0y=0 the scaled bounds force zero. Relaxing yyy represents convex combinations with the zero point by the same proof as above. The signed bounds are essential in general. Merely having two alternatives, without an explicit zero off-term, does not justify this elimination. Source: BGW, Eqs. (15.47)–(15.48), p. 521.

Cost assignment and logical scope¶

When exactly one indicator is selected, the disjunctive assignments c=γic=\gamma_ic=γi​ are equivalently expressed by c=∑iγiyic=\sum_i\gamma_i y_ic=∑i​γi​yi​. The equality takes the selected alternative’s cost. With several selected alternatives this expression instead adds their costs, so it must not be substituted into an inclusive-cost model without checking the intended semantics.

A separate complementarity warning concerns NLP solution methods. Biegler (2010), §11.3, p. 337, Eq. (11.18), gives 0≤x⊥(1−x)≥00\le x\perp(1-x)\ge00≤x⊥(1−x)≥0: the product condition x(1−x)=0x(1-x)=0x(1−x)=0 and the nonnegativity bounds leave only x=0x=0x=0 or x=1x=1x=1. The book warns that this disconnected feasible set can cause convergence difficulties and advises against using such MPCC constructions for exclusive choices. This is a warning about formulation and solution behavior, not a proof that complementarity cannot represent those two points. Inclusive alternatives can sometimes be modeled successfully with MPCCs, but the construction and its assumptions are problem dependent. The present lecture uses explicit binary/GDP selection instead. See MINLP Algorithms for the later discrete-continuous algorithm material.

Further reading and applications¶

The CNF procedure here follows BGW §15.7, pp. 515–516. BGW attribute its formalization to Clocksin & Mellish (1981). Raman & Grossmann (1991) connect logical inference with MILP process-synthesis modeling; the 1993 paper by Raman & Grossmann (1993) develops symbolic integration of logic, including CNF/DNF representations, in mixed-integer methods. These historical notes explain the relationship between the logic and algebraic models; they do not add another conversion algorithm to learn.

Start with Balas (1985) for disjunctive relaxations, Raman & Grossmann (1994) for the logic-based GDP framework, and Grossmann & Ruiz (2012) for formulations and alternative MINLP algorithms. Grossmann (2002) and Trespalacios & Grossmann (2014) are broader reviews; Kronqvist et al. (2026) give a historical overview. Grossmann & Trespalacios (2013) explain systematic discrete-continuous modeling, and Chen & Grossmann (2019) discuss model variants and hierarchy. Perez & Grossmann (2024) extend GDP to hierarchical structures and first-order logic. These are extension readings, not prerequisites for the bounded linear hull proof.

Representative applications include power/desalination superstructures (Mussati et al. (2008)), thermally linked distillation (Caballero & Grossmann (2001)), production scheduling (Castro & Grossmann (2012)), maintenance scheduling (Castro et al. (2014)), solvent-mixture design (Jonuzaj et al. (2016)), modular process synthesis (Chen & Grossmann (2019)), and discrete-continuous energy-system model predictive control (Bhattacharya et al. (2021)).

Nonlinear solution methods are developed by Lee & Grossmann (2005); Türkay & Grossmann (1996) treat discontinuous investment costs and multiple size regions. The current Pyomo modeling ecosystem is described by Chen et al. (2022).

Biegler (2010), Nonlinear Programming: Concepts, Algorithms, and Applications, §11.3, p. 337 (complementarity warning). Postek et al.
